description: Width tiers for HASS Year 3 — ACARA v9. One entry per descriptor. K-strand descriptors use phenomena_contexts; S-strand descriptors use task_contexts.
subject: HASS

width_notes.minimum_width: For K-strand (Knowledge) descriptors: the narrowest set of phenomena or contexts that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For S-strand (Skills/Inquiry) descriptors: the narrowest task context in which the skill is applied.
width_notes.typical_width: For K-strand descriptors: engagement across the elaboration range. For S-strand descriptors: the skill practised across two or more task types or contexts representative of the elaboration scope.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new phenomena, cultural contexts, or task contexts. First Nations elaborations always appear in wider where present in ACARA source material.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as source data. First Nations elaborations consistently placed in wider.

AC9HS3K01.minimum_width: Identify one cause and one effect of a change to the local community and describe how a person or group contributed to that change.
AC9HS3K01.typical_width: Investigate causes and effects of multiple types of change in the local community — transport, environment, built landscape, social composition — using sources such as photographs, oral histories and newspapers; identify individuals and groups from diverse backgrounds who contributed to community development.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians contributed to the character of the local community, including through environmental management, cultural influence or presence before and after European settlement
Compare two different types of local community change — for example, a built environment change and a social/demographic change — to identify whether their causes and effects are similar or different
elaborations: exploring photographs, newspapers, oral histories, diaries and letters to investigate how an aspect of life in the local community, such as transport, entertainment, the natural and built environment, and technologies, has changed over time; for example, from the time of European settlement to the present day

comparing photographs from the past and present of a specific location to identify the change or continuity (similarities and differences over time) associated with people, events or developments, places or ecosystems
identifying individuals and groups of diverse backgrounds from the past, who have contributed to the community's economic, social, cultural, civic and environmental development and character
investigating reasons for change in the local community, why change was brought about and what happened because of it; for example, the change in use of a building, wasteland turning to wetland

AC9HS3K02.minimum_width: Identify one significant Australian event or commemoration, describe its historical origins and explain why it matters.
AC9HS3K02.typical_width: Identify and discuss a range of significant Australian celebrations, commemorations, symbols and emblems — including Australia Day, Anzac Day, NAIDOC Week, National Sorry Day and major religious and cultural festivals; explain their origins, use and significance; recognise that people hold different views about some commemorations.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' flags and commemorations — including NAIDOC Week, National Sorry Day and Mabo Day — represent distinct historical experiences, and examine the protocols around flying First Nations Australian flags alongside the Australian flag

Examine why the same event (such as Australia Day) can be interpreted differently by different groups, including First Nations Australians who regard it as 'Invasion Day', and how these different perspectives reflect different historical experiences
elaborations: identifying and discussing the historical origins of an important Australian celebration or commemoration, including Australia Day, Anzac Day, NAIDOC Week and National Sorry Day, as well as significant religious or cultural festivals, such as Easter, Christmas, Lunar New Year, Diwali and Eid

recognising that people have different points of view on some events that are commemorated and celebrated; for example, some First Nations Australians regard "Australia Day" as "Invasion Day" and many non-Christians celebrate Christmas

generating a list of local, state/territory, national and religious symbols and emblems (for example, the Commonwealth Coat of Arms, the Australian Flag and First Nations Australians' flags, state/territory flags and coats of arms, club emblems, school logos, flags, floral emblems, and religious symbols, such as the Christian cross, the Crescent and Star, and the Magen David), and discussing their origins, use and significance

examining the symbolism found in the design and positioning of flags (for example, the Australian flag, First Nations Australians' flags) and recognising special occasions when they are flown (for example, all three flags are flown during NAIDOC Week, National Reconciliation Week, National Sorry Day and Mabo Day)
examining the roles, rights and responsibilities the community has when observing protocols around flag flying

AC9HS3K03.minimum_width: Locate and name the states and territories of Australia and their capital cities on a map.
AC9HS3K03.typical_width: Use geographical tools to locate Australian states, territories and capitals, as well as neighbouring countries (Pacific Island nations, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, Indonesia); identify their direction from Australia; represent Australia as both surveyed states/territories and as Aboriginal Countries and Torres Strait Islander Places.
wider: Compare the boundaries of Aboriginal Countries and Torres Strait Islander Places (using the AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia) with surveyed state and territory boundaries, investigating why these two representations of Australia differ so significantly
Investigate the geographical features and relative scale of two or more of Australia's neighbouring countries, explaining how their location shapes Australia's regional relationships
elaborations: using geographical tools to locate and name the states and territories in Australia, along with their capital cities; for example, a globe, wall map or digital source such as an online satellite image

using a globe or digital source to locate the Pacific Island nations, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, Indonesia and countries relevant to students, labelling them on a map and identifying the direction of each country from Australia

using the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies Map of Indigenous Australia and a states and territories map of Australia to compare the boundaries of Aboriginal Countries and Torres Strait Islander Places with the surveyed boundaries between Australian states and territories, to gain an appreciation of the different ways Australia can be represented

AC9HS3K04.minimum_width: Explain one way that First Nations Australians in a specific part of Australia are interconnected with Country/Place.
AC9HS3K04.typical_width: Describe multiple ways First Nations Australians connect to Country/Place — through birth, family, residence, and chosen or forced movement; explore these connections through poems, songs, paintings and stories from different groups across Australia.
wider: Investigate how some First Nations Australians hold connections to more than one Country/Place — for example through marriage, birth, parents or residence — and how this differs from non-Indigenous understandings of belonging to a single place
Compare how First Nations Australians from contrasting regions (for example, a coastal and an inland group) express their connections to Country/Place through different creative and cultural forms
elaborations: explaining that some First Nations Australians have special connections to many Countries/Places; for example, through marriage, birth, parents, residence and chosen or forced movement, and that First Nations Australians can identify with more than one Country/Place
discussing how some people are connected to one Country; for example, because it is "Mother's" Country or "Father's" Country
exploring the ways Australian First Nations Peoples connect to Country/Place, by reading and viewing poems, songs, paintings and stories from different groups outside the local area

AC9HS3K05.minimum_width: Identify one similarity and one difference in natural features between a place in Australia and a place in a neighbouring country.
AC9HS3K05.typical_width: Identify and describe similarities and differences between places in Australia and neighbouring countries in natural features (climate, landforms, vegetation, animal life), managed features and constructed features; investigate how climate shapes housing and settlement patterns.
wider: Compare the main climate types found in Australia and a neighbouring country (for example, equatorial zones in Indonesia, tropical zones in Papua New Guinea) and investigate how climate shapes natural vegetation, animal life and human settlement in each

Investigate settlement hierarchies — from isolated dwellings to large cities — in both Australia and a neighbouring country, identifying how environmental and economic factors shape where and how people settle
elaborations: identifying and locating examples of the main climatic types in Australia and neighbouring countries (for example, equatorial, tropical arid, semi-arid, temperate) and the features of those climate types and their impact on other natural features

identifying and describing the similarities and differences between places in Australia and places in neighbouring countries, such as Indonesia and Pacific Island nations, in their natural features; for example, rocks, landforms, bodies of water, climate, soils, natural vegetation and animal life
investigating differences in the type of housing that people use in different climates and environments
exploring different types of settlement and classifying them into hierarchical categories, such as isolated dwellings, outstations, villages, towns, regional centres and large cities

choosing a place in a neighbouring country, such as Indonesia or Pacific Island nations, to compare with a place in Australia in terms of managed and built features to explore the reasons for similarities and differences

AC9HS3K06.minimum_width: Identify who makes rules in one familiar context and explain why rules are important in that context.
AC9HS3K06.typical_width: Examine who makes rules in different contexts (parents, teachers, coaches, community), why rules differ across contexts, and what happens when rules are not followed; discuss situations where one rule cannot fairly apply to everyone.
wider: Explore how cultural norms behind rulemaking differ — for example, protocols around removing shoes before entering places of cultural or religious significance — and what this reveals about how rules reflect community values
Investigate how rules protect the rights of students with disability or different needs, examining cases where a fair rule must differ across individuals rather than treating everyone the same
elaborations: developing and justifying a set of fair rules and consequences for the class
identifying familiar rules, how rules protect the rights of others, what their responsibilities are to others, and the consequences when rules are not followed

exploring who has the authority to make rules in different contexts (for example, parents, teachers, coaches) and considering why rules differ across these contexts, such as a school playground, in class, at home, or in sport

discussing situations where it is not fair to have one rule that treats everyone the same; for example, if some people, such as students with disability, have different needs or would be unable to follow the rules
exploring cultural norms behind some rulemaking; for example, removing shoes before entering places of cultural or religious significance

AC9HS3K07.minimum_width: Identify one community group or individual who actively participates in the local community and explain their purpose.
AC9HS3K07.typical_width: Identify and describe a range of community groups and individuals who participate in local, school and virtual communities; explore motivations for participation including volunteering, leadership, and recognition such as an Order of Australia award.
wider: Investigate how community Elders and First Nations Australian community leaders contribute to their communities, comparing their roles with those of mainstream community volunteers or local government representatives
Explore participation in a specific school or community project — for example, supporting a conservation or aid effort — and evaluate how individual contributions combine to achieve collective impact
elaborations: identifying groups that actively participate in the local community or through a virtual community and exploring their purpose

exploring how they could participate in a school or community project; for example, raising money for a relevant aid project, such as supporting disadvantaged communities overseas or working to protect a bird habitat
investigating how an individual's contribution can be recognised; for example, an Order of Australia award
exploring the motivations of individuals who contribute to communities, such as local community volunteers, leaders and Elders

AC9HS3S01.minimum_width: Develop at least one inquiry question to guide an investigation about a place, person, event or issue.
AC9HS3S01.typical_width: Develop a range of inquiry questions across question types — 'Why there?' location questions; 'What might happen?' consequence questions; 'What ought to happen?' ethical questions; comparative questions — to guide an investigation.
wider: Develop probing follow-up questions during an investigation (for example, 'Why is that so?', 'What else do we need to know?') rather than only planning questions at the start
Generate questions that address disciplinary concepts — cause, significance, change, location, sustainability, rules — demonstrating awareness of what each concept requires as an inquiry focus
elaborations: developing inquiring questions as they investigate; for example, "Why there?" questions about location; "What might happen?" questions about future consequences of natural processes or people's actions in places; and "What ought to happen?" questions or other questions about ethical behaviour, sustainability and preferred futures
asking probing questions during an investigation (for example, "Why is that so?", "What else do we need to know?")
posing questions to compare such as "How have things changed?" and "How is my house the same or different to one in a neighbouring country?"

AC9HS3S02.minimum_width: Locate and record information from one provided source type relevant to an investigation.
AC9HS3S02.typical_width: Locate and collect information from a range of source types — photographs, interviews, satellite images, field observations, digital maps; record findings using annotated timelines, annotated maps and tables or graphs.
wider: Collect information through field observation (photographs, sketches, interviews) and then cross-reference with archival or digital sources, identifying what each method of data collection adds

Gather and record geographical information from a geographically contrasting school or community, constructing and annotating maps with appropriate cartographic conventions (title, symbols, north point)
elaborations: locating sources suited to learning about the past, such as photographs, interviews, newspapers, digital media, stories, cemetery observations, interviews with older people, and maps, including those online

collecting information in the field; for example, taking photographs, making sketches or collecting natural objects, or interviewing or surveying people to seek information about feelings, preferences, perspectives and actions
gathering information from maps, aerial photographs, satellite images or digital application objects, to support the investigation of the natural, managed and constructed features of places
sequencing information about local people and events in annotated timelines to show change

acquiring geographical information from schools in geographically contrasting parts of Australia and neighbouring countries and recording that information by constructing and annotating maps, using the appropriate cartographic conventions, including map symbols, title and north point
creating tables or picture and column graphs to show patterns in data collected from class vote on participation in community activities

AC9HS3S03.minimum_width: Interpret information displayed in one format — for example, a map, graph or photograph — and identify one key finding.
AC9HS3S03.typical_width: Interpret information displayed across multiple formats — climate data, maps (ground, aerial, digital), graphs, tables, photographs — to identify patterns, make comparisons and describe features of places and past events.
wider: Interpret two different data formats about the same topic (for example, a map and a climate graph for the same place) and identify what each reveals that the other does not
Distinguish between fiction and non-fiction sources about the same place or period, explaining how each type of source is useful and where each has limitations
elaborations: distinguishing between fiction and non-fiction texts in relation to representation of places, environments and past events
interpreting climate data to describe the temperature and rainfall for a place in Australia and a place in a neighbouring country
interpreting information about the number of parents that volunteer at the school and why they may choose to contribute in this way
interpreting data to identify patterns of change over time: for example, examine building dates to make inferences about changing designs and materials used

using maps, ground and aerial photographs, and a digital source such as online satellite images to identify, locate and describe features, including the interpretation of cartographic information such as titles, map symbols, north point and compass direction

AC9HS3S04.minimum_width: Compare information from two sources to identify evidence of change or different perspectives on one topic.
AC9HS3S04.typical_width: Analyse information across multiple sources — historical images, maps, interviews with diverse community members — to identify evidence of change, effects of events, and different perspectives on rules, development or community life.
wider: Analyse information collected from interviews with different community members (children, teachers, Elders, coaches) about the same issue — such as rules — and identify how role or position shapes each perspective
Use visible thinking strategies to examine a sequence of maps or images across time, identifying both what has changed and what patterns of continuity remain across the local area
elaborations: comparing information in different sources to identify evidence of change; for example, images and maps of the local area over time
comparing different accounts of historic events to determine the effects of changes; for example, how the development of local farming or industry impacted on people and the environment
analysing information collected from interviews with different people, such as children, teachers, coaches and community members, about rules and how decisions are made
using visible thinking strategies to examine a group of paintings and/or maps across a period of time, to explore evidence of continuity and change, and significant events in the local area

AC9HS3S05.minimum_width: Draw one conclusion based on analysis of collected information about change, place or community.
AC9HS3S05.typical_width: Draw conclusions grounded in data analysis about how a place or community has changed, the preservation of natural features, and the connections between people and places in Australia and neighbouring countries.
wider: Draw conclusions that integrate findings across two or more topic areas — for example, connecting community change to environmental change — rather than drawing separate conclusions for each
Evaluate whether a conclusion drawn early in an investigation needs to be revised in light of additional evidence collected later
elaborations: reaching conclusions about how their place and community have changed and developed based on an analysis of data and information related to settlement patterns, local changes in plant and animal species, historic events or cultural celebrations
drawing conclusions about the preservation of unique features of the natural environment
drawing conclusions about the ways people are connected with places, and the similarities and differences of places in Australia and those of neighbouring countries

AC9HS3S06.minimum_width: Propose one action in response to a community challenge and identify a likely effect of that action.
AC9HS3S06.typical_width: Propose actions or responses across different issue types — environmental, civic, cultural — anticipating effects; develop a plan to achieve a specific goal such as protecting a place, participating in a community event, or raising awareness.
wider: Argue a point of view on a civics and citizenship issue — for example, consequences of breaking school rules, the value of community contribution — using persuasive language effectively to seek support from others
Evaluate proposed actions by identifying possible negative as well as positive effects, and selecting or modifying the proposal based on that evaluation
elaborations: contributing ideas to a group response to a community challenge; for example, ways their class or school could contribute to recycling or conserving energy

considering anticipated effects of actions designed to protect and improve places that people perceive as important, such as places of environmental, cultural or religious value, or historic significance

developing a plan of action to achieve a set goal; for example, to protect a place, to participate in a community festival or commemoration, to raise awareness about an issue, to raise money for a purpose

arguing a point of view on a civics and citizenship issue relevant to their lives (for example, the consequences of breaking school rules, the value of contributing to their community, the need to preserve an endangered species) and making effective use of persuasive language such as "I think" and "I dis/agree that" to gain the support of others

AC9HS3S07.minimum_width: Present a description or explanation using ideas from at least one source and at least one subject-specific term correctly.
AC9HS3S07.typical_width: Present descriptions and explanations using ideas drawn from graphs, tables, timelines, photographs and pictures; apply historical, geographical and civics terms accurately across speaking, writing and illustration.
wider: Present findings that combine multiple subject areas — for example, a response that uses historical, geographical and civics terms together to explain a community issue — rather than drawing on vocabulary from a single discipline
Present to an audience beyond the classroom (family, community members) using accurate subject-specific terms and visual sources, adapting the communication for a non-specialist audience
elaborations: selecting ideas from sources such as graphs, tables, timelines, photographs and pictures

using appropriate terms when speaking, writing and illustrating; for example, historical terms such as "immigration", "exploration", "development", "settlement", "naming days of commemoration" and "emblems"; geographical terms such as "climate", "environment", "natural" and "constructed"; and civics terms such as "community", "decision-making" and "participation"
